lesson.title: What a P-Value Actually Tells You (and What It Doesn't)
lesson.summary: A p-value measures the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis, but it is easy to misstate what it means, and getting the wording exactly right matters as much as getting the number right.
lesson.body:
It helps to see the common wrong interpretations laid out next to the right one, because the wrong versions sound almost reasonable until you check them against the actual definition. Wrong: "the p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true." This is backwards, the p-value is computed by assuming H0 is true from the start, so it cannot also tell you the chance that H0 is true, that would require a different kind of reasoning entirely, using information the p-value calculation never touches. Wrong: "the p-value is the probability the result happened by random chance." This is too vague, it specifically measures the chance of a result this extreme or more extreme, given H0, not some general sense that the whole study might be a fluke. Wrong: "a large p-value proves the null hypothesis is true." A large p-value only means the data do not contradict H0, and the same data would often be just as consistent with many nearby parameter values, not proof of any single one. Right: "assuming H0 is true, the probability of getting a sample result this extreme or more extreme, from natural sampling variability alone, is the p-value."

Apply that to the cereal box test, where p = 0.0456. The correct interpretation is: if the machine really is centered at 16 ounces, there is about a 4.56 percent chance that a random sample of 36 boxes would have a mean at least 0.1 ounces away from 16 just by chance. Compare that to a tempting but incorrect rewrite: "there is a 4.56 percent chance the true mean is 16 ounces." That sentence flips the conditional around, it treats the parameter as random and the data as fixed, when the calculation actually treated the null value as fixed and asked about the data.

A smaller p-value means stronger evidence against H0, but whether a given p-value counts as "small" is relative to a threshold chosen in advance, the significance level, covered next. It is also worth flagging a separate trap: a p-value says nothing directly about how large or practically important an effect is. A very small p-value can come from a tiny, practically unimportant difference if the sample size is large enough to detect it precisely, and a moderately large p-value can come from a real, meaningful difference if the sample is small and noisy. The p-value measures how incompatible the data are with H0, not how big or how important the underlying difference turns out to be, those are two different questions that a careful reader keeps separate.
